latest.question: Deputy Colm Burke asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the status of an application (details supplied); and when it is envisaged that same will be completed in view that it is four months since it was submitted.
latest.reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 99 and 100 together.
I can inform the Deputy that the applications cited continue to be processed by the EU Treaty Rights Division of my Department.
While every effort is made to issue a decision on each application as soon as possible, current processing times may vary having regard to the complexity of an application, the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances and whether further information is required. latest.question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the way in which his Department justifies the €29,432 temporary protection Transition scheme threshold for disabled applicants; and the reason the State is ignoring equality directives regarding this issue.
latest.reply:
The Temporary Protection Transition scheme was launched on 30 September 2026 in line with the EU Council recommendation for a co-ordinated approach to transition people from Temporary Protection across the EU.
People with Temporary Protection who wish to transition to the new permission must meet the eligibility criteria, including a minimum earnings requirement of €29,432 per year, have independent accommodation, and be resident in Ireland for a period of one year as a beneficiary of Temporary Protection prior to the opening of the new permission application process. The earnings threshold applies to all applicants seeking to avail of this alternative immigration permission.
Full details of the scheme and eligibility criteria are outlined in the Scheme Policy Document and FAQ document available online at www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/collections/a-new-permission-en/.
Ireland will continue to support people from Ukraine under Temporary Protection, to include those who are vulnerable or have barriers to independence. The alternative permission is not intended to replace Temporary Protection, but to provide an alternative permission for those who are eligible and who wish to remain in Ireland beyond its protection. Persons who do not apply or are unable to satisfy the eligibility criteria will continue to be entitled to and benefit from the Temporary Protection Status while the Temporary Protection Directive remains in effect.

latest.question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the current processing times for IRP card renewals; and the resources that are being deployed to ensure there are no undue delays.
latest.reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 96 and 97 together.
The Registration Office of my Department continues to experience high demand for both first-time registration appointments, and immigration permission renewal applications.
I understand that waiting times can be frustrating for applicants, and I can assure the Deputy that my Department is making every effort to facilitate as many applicants as possible and to increase processing capacity. Additional staff have been assigned to this work, resulting in a reduction in processing times for renewal applications.
I am pleased to inform the Deputy that, for certain categories of renewals, processing times are now approximately 5 weeks from the date of application, with no category currently exceeding a waiting time of 9 weeks.
While my Department endeavours to process applications as quickly as possible, processing times may vary due to a number of factors, such as the number of applications on hand, individual circumstances, the complexity of applications, whether further information is required, and peak application periods.

latest.question: Deputy Gary Gannon asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration the rationale for the continued application of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings; and whether his Department has assessed the effectiveness of the rule in protecting children and vulnerable parties.
latest.reply:
I propose to take Questions Nos. 92, 93, 94, 95 and 105 together.
Ensuring transparency and promoting a greater understanding of the family law system is critical to maintaining and building trust in it. At the same time, those who seek the assistance of the courts in resolving their family justice disputes need to be assured that their privacy, and that of their children, will be maintained at what can be a very difficult time. In recognising the need for a balance between these two positions, the Family Justice Strategy commits to undertaking a review of the operation of the in-camera rule in family law proceedings.
Further to this commitment, an independent research report, entitled The Operation of the In Camera Rule in Family Law Proceedings, was published in 2025. The extensive report contains 21 detailed recommendations. Officials from my Department are currently considering the findings and recommendations of the report in the context of developing policy proposals for reform. This detailed work is ongoing, and policy proposals for reform will be submitted to me for consideration when finalised. At the same time, such proposals will also consider how clarity can be provided regarding the scope of the rule and its impact for those involved in proceedings and enhance understanding of family law proceedings across society. latest.question: Deputy Emer Currie asked the Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration for an update on citizenship applications for persons (details supplied); and for a timeframe on a decision to be communicated.
latest.reply:
The naturalisation applications referred to by the Deputy continue to be processed by my Department.
These applications are based on Section 16 'Irish Association', which can take longer to process than applications based upon residency.
Section 15 of the Act sets out the statutory conditions that must be fulfilled for a certificate of naturalisation to be granted. Section 16 of the Act gives discretion to waive the statutory conditions (including the 5 year residency requirement) in certain circumstances. This includes where the applicant is a direct descendant of someone who is or was an Irish citizen (for example, a grandparent), has a family connection to an Irish citizen (including by blood, adoption, or civil partnership), or is related by affinity, meaning a close relationship through a spouse’s family.
Last year my Department published new guidelines for applications on the basis of Irish Associations under Section 16(1)(a) of the Irish Nationality and Citizenship Act 1956. They set out the factors that may be considered when deciding whether to waive the statutory conditions in certain circumstances, including where the applicant is of Irish descent or Irish associations. Details of the guidelines are available on my Department’s website at the following link: www.irishimmigration.ie/how-to-become-an-irish-citizen-guide/
As an Oireachtas member, you can also request the status of individual immigration cases by e-mail, using the Oireachtas Mail facility at: IMoireach

latest.question: Deputy Shónagh Ní Raghallaigh asked the Minister for Social Protection if it is possible for a person (details supplied), regarding any American pension entitlement, to use a portion of their Irish credits to make up the shortfall for the six quarters under the bilateral agreement; whether this would affect his Irish entitlements.
latest.reply:
The person concerned was awarded state pension contributory from their 66th birthday based on their Irish social insurance record.
The state pension contributory is currently in payment at the weekly rate of €293.50 which equates to 98% of the maximum personal rate.
Under the Bilateral Social Security Agreement between Ireland and the United States of America, insurance periods completed in one country may be taken into account by the other country for the purpose of establishing entitlement to certain social security benefits. Entitlement is determined separately by each country in accordance with its own legislation.
This process does not involve any transfer of social insurance contributions from one country to the other. Coverage in one country may be used to give entitlement to a pro rata pension in the other country. As a person's state pension contributory entitlement is based solely on their Irish social insurance record, any pension entitlement they may have from any other jurisdiction does not affect their rate of payment.
The agreement with the United States provides that where a person has completed at least six quarters of coverage under U.S. laws, but does not have sufficient coverage to qualify for a benefit from there, periods of coverage in Ireland could be used to establish entitlement. latest.question: Deputy Sean Fleming asked the Minister for Social Protection if an oral hearing and a date for same will be expedited in respect of an application for the State Pension (details supplied).
latest.reply:
The person concerned was in receipt of payment as a qualified adult on their spouse's State pension contributory from 12 November 2015 to 7 May 2026.
An Increase for Qualified Adult (IQA) is a means-tested allowance which may be paid where a claimant's spouse, civil partner or cohabitant is being wholly or mainly maintained by them and where the qualified adult's means do not exceed the prescribed limits.
Where a qualified adult has weekly means of up to €100, the maximum rate of IQA is payable. A reduced rate is payable where weekly means exceed €100 but do not exceed €310. Where weekly means exceed €310, there is no entitlement to an IQA payment. Where property or assets are held jointly, the qualified adult's means are assessed as half of the total amount. The family home is not included in the means assessment.
As part of the Department's ongoing programme of review to ensure that customers are receiving their correct entitlement, a review questionnaire issued to the spouse of the person concerned on 21 October 2025 seeking details on the means of the qualified adult.
Following examination of the information provided, it was established that the person concerned had weekly means of €735.78, arising primarily from capital held in joint bank accounts. As the means exceed the statutory limit for the IQA, a decision issued on 30 April 2026 advising that the IQA payment was being terminated.

latest.question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Social Protection his currents plans to address the issue of parents who are transgender not being recognised as the parents of their children.
latest.reply:
The legislation governing the registering of a birth is set out in the Civil Registration Act (2004). The required particulars of the parent(s) of a child to be recorded in the birth registration include the sex of the parent.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is female, that person can select "mother" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the person who gives birth to the child is male, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is female, that person can only select "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
Where the gender of the other parent is male, that person can select "father" or "parent" as their label on the child's birth certificate.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

examples.reply:
As previously advised to the Deputy, the school referred to was approved to enter my Department's pipeline of projects under the Additional School Accommodation (ASA) scheme.
The project received approval from my Department to commence construction in January 2026. More recently, Department officials were notified by the school authorities that construction has now commenced. Expected completion to coincide with the start of the new school year.

examples.question: Deputy Paul Donnelly asked the Minister for Defence if she is aware of Irish Defence Forces members participating in military competitions with the Israeli Defence Forces; and if confirmed, her views on such on participation.
examples.reply:
The Defence Forces participate in international military competitions in order to promote in the Defence Forces the adoption of international best practice, exchange of tactics, techniques and procedures (TTP) and encourage the development of military skills. It also contributes to the development of particular military skillsets and doctrines.
The decision on who to invite to these competitions lies with the hosting nation. I am informed by the military authorities that the Defence Forces have not participated in any military competitions organised by the Israeli Defence Forces. I am also informed that, to date, no Defence Forces team has reported Israeli Defence Forces participation in competitions attended by Defence Forces personnel.

examples.question: Deputy Erin McGreehan asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine for an update on the timeline and commencement dates for the basic income support for sustainability scheme.
examples.reply:
My Department is fully committed to making payments to farmers under the various schemes at the earliest date possible and to the maximum number of farmers possible. This commitment to farmers is evidenced in the very high payment rates achieved across all schemes over the last number of years in both EU and Exchequer funded schemes.
The timelines for all schemes, including the planned payment dates, have been set after extensive consultation with farmers and taking account of application systems, monitoring systems, validation and processing systems and payment systems.
In 2025, my Department commenced payments under the Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS) scheme from October 16th ensuring money flowed as soon as practically possible to farmers.
This payment date is in line with the traditional payment date of the BISS Scheme to farmers and is as outlined in the Farmers' Charter.

examples.question: Deputy Tom Brabazon asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage for an update on the financial contribution scheme; and the rationale to no longer fund this scheme.
examples.reply:
The Government’s new housing plan, Delivering Homes, Building Communities 2025-2030, includes measures to increase delivery of housing for older people through increased delivery of social housing, increased delivery of more suitable homes in private housing and increased choice to support voluntary rightsizing, including a review of the operation of existing local authority financial contribution schemes.
I understand that existing financial contribution schemes in place in some local authorities are non-statutory and therefore a matter for the individual local authorities. Consideration will be given to a review of the operation of existing local authority financial contribution schemes and my Department is advancing these measures now incorporated in the new housing plan.

examples.question: Deputy Réada Cronin asked the Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment what specific regulatory changes are being sought by Re-Turn for the proposed rPET reprocessing facility; the Department's position on the establishment of such a processing facility.
examples.reply:
Re-turn is a producer-led and owned, not-for-profit company established by beverage producers to meet their obligations under the Separate Collection (Deposit Return Scheme) Regulations.
Re-turn has stated its ambition to develop an rPET reprocessing facility in Ireland. In this regard, Re-turn has briefed me and Departmental officials on its plans.
The matter remains under consideration, with the Department considering the various public policy considerations that arise.

examples.question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Transport further to Parliamentary Question No.199 of 16 April 2026, regarding Ireland's current position (details supplied); whether he has articulated this position either internally with Irish officials or with European counterparts; if so, if he will provide details of what was articulated and through which medium.
examples.reply:
I am aware of the concerns raised by car rental fleet operators regarding the Clean Corporate Vehicles proposal. We engage regularly with representatives from this sector and have met with them several times over the past year, including discussions specifically on this proposal.
It should be noted that the measure remains at proposal stage, with negotiations currently underway at EU level. The Regulation will not be finalised until such time as an agreement is reached between the Council and the European Parliament. This process is expected to run through 2026, which intersects with Ireland’s Presidency of the Council of the EU.

examples.question: Deputy Paul Murphy asked the Minister for Agriculture, Food and the Marine the numerical, scientific and editorial verification carried out before the Wildlife Unit End of Year Report for 2025 that was approved for publication; whether further errors have since been identified; and whether his Department will publish an amended report clearly identifying all corrections.
examples.reply:
The Wildlife Report compiled by my Department has stated that there was 7,625 badger captures in the vaccine area in 2025. This is the correct figure. The figure of 8,123 is the number of badger captures that were recorded in vaccine areas for 2024. Table 4 in the report states the correct figures of badger captures for 2024 and 2025.
For the purposes of clarity the figure for 2024 will be removed from the body of the text.

examples.question: Deputy Carol Nolan asked the Minister for Social Protection the number of people who have had their receipt of jobseeker's allowance or jobseeker's benefit permanently withdrawn or revoked for breach of the conditions associated with their claim, and who have not subsequently had their claim reinstated, from January 2020 to date.
examples.reply:
To be eligible for a Jobseeker's payment a person must satisfy all the eligibility criteria for the relevant scheme.
Where a claim has been stopped, it will only be re-instated following an application by the customer and where all conditions of the scheme are satisfied.
It is not possible to provide data on the number of claims stopped and not subsequently re-instated due to the large churn on jobseekers schemes and the many legitimate reasons that claims are stopped.
I trust that this clarifies matters for the Deputy.

examples.question: Deputy Ruth Coppinger asked the Minister for Social Protection the annual figures since 2015 for appeals lodged with the social welfare appeals office querying a refusal based on the habitual residence condition, by Irish citizens and non-Irish nationals, in tabular form.
examples.reply:
I am advised by the Chief Appeals Officer that the Social Welfare Appeals Office does not collate data on appeals specifically relating to the Habitual Residence Condition, therefore the statistical information is not available.
I trust this clarifies the matter for the Deputy.

examples.question: Deputy John Paul O'Shea asked the Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage the number of appeals involving the rating of agricultural or horticultural buildings have been brought before the Valuation Tribunal since 2020; the number that were successful; and the average length of time taken to determine these appeals.
examples.reply:
As the Valuation Tribunal is independent in the performance of its functions, my Department does not hold the information requested in relation to the number of appeals involving the rating of agricultural or horticultural buildings have been brought before the Valuation Tribunal since 2020; the number that were successful; or the average length of time taken to determine these appeals.
It is noted that certain information on Valuation Tribunal appeals activity is included in the Tribunal's Annual Reports, available on the organisation's website at: www.valuationtribunal.ie/about-us/publications/.
Judgements of the Valuation Tribunal are also published and can be accessed on the Tribunal's website (at: www.valuationtribunal.ie/judgments/) under 'Name', 'Year', 'Property category' and 'Rating Authority'. It is noted that the Tribunal does not, however, include a specific category of appeal termed 'agriculture / horticultural'.
The Deputy may wish to contact the Tribunal directly in relation to the information sought by emailing info@valuationtribunal.ie.

examples.question: Deputy Paul Lawless asked the Minister for Transport for a record of all reported accidents, collisions, or safety incidents that have occurred at or in the vicinity of the unmarked traffic islands in Ballindine, County Mayo, on the N17, over the past 20 years; if road safety audits or assessments have been carried out at this location; and if there are plans to install appropriate road markings or safety measures at this site.
examples.reply:
As Minister for Transport, I have responsibility for overall policy and exchequer funding in relation to the National Roads Programme. Under the Roads Acts 1993-2015 and in line with the National Development Plan (NDP), the operation and management of individual national roads is a matter for Transport Infrastructure Ireland (TII), in conjunction with the local authorities concerned. This is also subject to the Infrastructure Guidelines and the necessary statutory approvals. In this context, TII is best placed to advise you in relation to safety on the N17 at Ballindine, Co. Mayo.
The Government is committed to reducing road deaths and creating safer roads for everyone in Ireland.
Noting the above position, I have referred your question to TII for a direct reply. Please advise my private office if you do not receive a reply within 10 working days.
